And I recounted to him the whole vision which I had seen, and he said unto me: ‘A terrible thing hast thou seen, my son, and of grave moment is thy dream-vision as to the secrets of all the sin of the earth: it must sink into the abyss and be destroyed with a great destruction.
My son, from heaven all this will come upon the earth, and upon the earth there will be great destruction.’

‘‹Go to Noah and› tell him in my name “Hide thyself!”, and reveal to him the end that is approaching: that the whole earth will be destroyed, and a deluge is about to come upon the whole earth, and will destroy all that is on it.

plain: The claim is that a cosmic impact around 12,000 years ago, at the time called the Younger Dryas near the end of the last ice age, brought on the great flood and wiped out an earlier civilisation, so that the world's flood myths would be memories of a real catastrophe. The podcaster Joe Rogan says on the show that nothing could stop such a strike and that "that's probably what happened during the younger dryas impact". Michels's pseudonymous co-host Jack, who says he has worked for years in defence and aerospace, mentions in passing "the Randall Carlson stuff and the Graham Hancock stuff, the reset 12,000 years ago", crediting the researcher Randall Carlson and the writer Graham Hancock, without naming any impact or flood. Rogan points to old texts, though not to particular passages. If he means the flood on the Eleventh Tablet of the Gilgamesh epic, in E. A. Wallis Budge's 1920 translation, the gods resolve "to make a wind-storm", "A black cloud from the foundation of heaven came up", and the Anunnaki, whom Budge glosses as star-gods of the southern sky, "brandished their torches" and "With their glare they lighted up the land"; that is the tablet's nearest image to fire from the sky, and reading it as an impact is a step the tablet neither states nor excludes. If he means the Book of Enoch, in R. H. Charles's 1917 translation, Enoch dreams that "the heaven collapsed and was borne off and fell to the earth" and the earth "was swallowed up in a great abyss", and elsewhere Noah is warned that "a deluge is about to come upon the whole earth". The book tells this as a judgement for sin; reading the falling heaven as an impact memory is the teller's step, which the text neither states nor excludes.

discussion.by: The Epic of Gilgamish, Tablet XI (translated by E. A. Wallis Budge in The Babylonian Story of the Deluge)
discussion.text: The teller does not say which part of the epic he means; if it is the flood of the Eleventh Tablet, the source says the great gods resolved "to make a wind-storm" and tells a rain-flood, "A black cloud from the foundation of heaven came up" in which Adad thundered, while the Anunnaki, whom the translator glosses as "The star-gods of the southern sky", "brandished their torches" and "With their glare they lighted up the land". Star-gods lighting up the land with torches is the tablet's nearest image to fire from the sky; reading the flood as the memory of an impact is a step the tablet neither states nor excludes. The words are from E. A. Wallis Budge's translation (The Babylonian Story of the Deluge, 1920) of the Eleventh Tablet of the Assyrian version, in which Uta-Napishtim tells Gilgamish of the flood.

discussion.by: The Book of Enoch (translated by R. H. Charles)
discussion.text: The teller names the Book of Enoch beside Ezekiel for its strange depictions and does not say which passage he means; if it is Enoch's first dream-vision, which the translator heads as a vision on the Deluge, the book tells how "the heaven collapsed and was borne off and fell to the earth" and "the earth was swallowed up in a great abyss" (83:3 to 4), and has Mahalalel read the dream as "the secrets of all the sin of the earth: it must sink into the abyss and be destroyed with a great destruction" (83:7). Where the book tells the flood itself it is a judgement announced to Noah, "a deluge is about to come upon the whole earth" (10:2). The book tells the destruction as a judgement for sin; reading the falling heaven as the memory of an impact at the Younger Dryas is the teller's step, which the text neither states nor excludes.
